---
title: "Health status in Portugal"
subtitle: "How long and how well people live, what they die of, which risk factors weigh most, and how access and resources have changed"
lang: en
---

::: {.callout-note}
This report uses only official INE and Eurostat data stored in the repository. Every number,
fact, event or link is marked in the text and has a row in `claims.csv`, with the source, the
access date and a short excerpt. All links between changes in the series and events are grade C:
they indicate coincidence in time, never cause.
:::

```{ojs}
Plotly = require("plotly.js-dist-min@2.35.2")
```

```{ojs}
import {timeSeries, smallMultiples, ranking, dumbbell, heatmap, dataTable} from "../../assets/charts.js"
```

```{ojs}
lang = "en"
```

```{ojs}
linked_events = FileAttachment("linked_events.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
nuts_regions = ["Portugal", "Norte", "Centro", "Grande Lisboa", "Península de Setúbal", "Oeste e Vale do Tejo", "Alentejo", "Algarve", "Região Autónoma dos Açores", "Região Autónoma da Madeira"]
```

```{ojs}
dedupe = (rows, key) => { const seen = new Set(); return rows.filter((r) => { const k = key(r); if (seen.has(k)) return false; seen.add(k); return true; }); }
```

```{ojs}
region_labels = ({"European Union (27)": "EU-27", "Região Autónoma dos Açores": "Azores (aut. region)", "Região Autónoma da Madeira": "Madeira (aut. region)", "Área Metropolitana de Lisboa": "Lisbon Metro Area"})
```

```{ojs}
sex_labels = ({HM: "Total", H: "Men", M: "Women"})
```

```{ojs}
year_table = (rows, groupBy, labels = {}) => { const groups = [...new Set(rows.map((r) => r[groupBy]))]; const names = groups.map((g) => labels[g] || g); const dates = [...new Set(rows.map((r) => r.date))].sort(); const fmt = (v) => v.toLocaleString("en-GB", {maximumFractionDigits: 2}); return dataTable(dates.map((dt) => Object.fromEntries([["Year", dt.slice(0, 4)], ...groups.map((g, i) => { const r = rows.find((q) => q[groupBy] === g && q.date === dt); return [names[i], r ? fmt(r.value) : "—"]; })])), ["Year", ...names]); }
```

## Summary

People in Portugal now live longer than at any point in the series: life expectancy at birth rose
from [64.0 years in 1960]{.claim id="c001"} to [82.5 years in 2024]{.claim id="c002"}, which is
[one year above the EU average in 2024]{.claim id="c006"}. The part of life spent without limitations
has also grown: healthy life years at birth rose from [53.9 in 2004]{.claim id="c025"} to
[64.8 in 2024]{.claim id="c026"}, and the gap to the EU shrank from [9.0 years]{.claim id="c029"}
to [0.4 years]{.claim id="c030"}.

Age-standardised mortality from diseases of the circulatory system fell from
[321.67 deaths per hundred thousand inhabitants in 2011]{.claim id="c040"} to [220.81 in 2023]{.claim id="c041"},
and infant mortality dropped from [77.5 per thousand live births in 1960]{.claim id="c082"} to
[3.0 in 2024]{.claim id="c083"}. Mortality from respiratory diseases remains above the European
average ([95.48 versus 75.18 per hundred thousand in 2023]{.claim id="c046"}).

There are also less favourable signs. The share of people reporting a chronic condition rose from
[32.1% in 2004]{.claim id="c095"} to [44.1% in 2025]{.claim id="c096"}, with a good part of the rise
concentrated in a few years early in the last decade, where an effect of the survey method cannot be
ruled out. Unmet dental care needs ([7.9% in 2025]{.claim id="c145"}) are more than double those
of the EU ([3.3%]{.claim id="c146"}). Households' out-of-pocket payments account for
[28.67% of current health expenditure in 2024]{.claim id="c162"}, against
[15.06% in the EU]{.claim id="c163"}.

The detection of trend changes was redone with a corrected detector and found
[29 candidate breaks: 10 coincided with verified events, in 12 links all of grade C, and 19 were left without an event]{.claim id="c210"}.
The events with a coincidence are the adjustment programme, the revision of user charges and the
pandemic; no source consulted establishes cause. None of the exploratory associations between
indicators survived the correction for multiple testing
([see Associations between indicators]{.claim id="c209"}). Weekly excess mortality during the
pandemic was not covered for lack of a tested source ([see Question 5]{.claim id="c094"}).

## Question 1 — Life expectancy at birth and at age 65

Life expectancy at birth in Portugal grew almost continuously from
[1960, when it was 64.0 years]{.claim id="c001"}, to [2024, with 82.5 years]{.claim id="c002"}. The
robust trend estimate points to [an increase of about 0.30 years per calendar year, an increasing trend (Theil-Sen, Mann-Kendall)]{.claim id="c017"}.
The EU average, available since the start of the century, rose more slowly:
[about 0.16 years per year, also with an increasing trend]{.claim id="c018"}.

Portugal went from slightly below the European average, with [77.4 years in 2002]{.claim id="c004"}
against [77.6 years in the EU]{.claim id="c003"}, to above it: [82.5 years]{.claim id="c002"} against
[81.5 years in the EU in 2024]{.claim id="c005"}, [a difference of 1.0 year in Portugal's favour]{.claim id="c006"}.

Women live longer than men. At the start of the series, life expectancy at birth was
[66.7 years for women in 1960]{.claim id="c009"} and [61.1 years for men]{.claim id="c010"};
at the end it was [85.2 years for women in 2024]{.claim id="c007"} and [79.7 years for men]{.claim id="c008"}.

[At age 65, life expectancy went from 13.6 years in 1960]{.claim id="c011"} to
[21.1 years in 2024]{.claim id="c012"}, above the European average ([20.2 years in 2024]{.claim id="c013"}).

In the first years of the pandemic the series fell back: from [82.0 years in 2019]{.claim id="c014"} to
[81.4 years in 2020]{.claim id="c015"} and [81.4 years in 2021]{.claim id="c016"}. The study does not
attribute a cause to this decline; without excess mortality data (Question 5), it cannot be
decomposed. The only breaks found in this series date from the 1960s and 1970s and were left without
an associated event (see Trend changes and events).

```{ojs}
le_data = FileAttachment("q01_life_expectancy.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof le_sex = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Total", "T"], ["Women", "F"], ["Men", "M"]]), {value: "T", label: "Sex"})
```

```{ojs}
viewof le_age = Inputs.radio(new Map([["At birth", "0"], ["At age 65", "65"]]), {value: "0", label: "Age"})
```

```{ojs}
smallMultiples(Plotly, le_data.filter((d) => d.sex === le_sex && String(d.age) === le_age), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, cols: 2, yTitle: "Life expectancy (years)", lang, alt: "Two panels with the same axis, Portugal since 1960 and the EU since 2002, showing life expectancy: an almost continuous rise, Portugal overtaking the European average and a small dip in 2020."})
```

*Chart: life expectancy at birth and at age sixty-five, one panel for Portugal and one for the EU, with the same vertical axis (Eurostat).*

### Regional differences

INE regional data are calculated in three-year periods, and each point corresponds to the period
starting in the year shown. In the most recent period of the series, life expectancy at birth ranged from
[78.04 years in the Autonomous Region of the Azores]{.claim id="c020"} to
[81.53 years in the Norte]{.claim id="c019"}, with [Madeira at 78.77 years]{.claim id="c022"}. The
autonomous regions remain at the bottom of the table, but they are the ones that have risen most: the
Azores started from [75.86 years in the period beginning in 2008]{.claim id="c021"}, with
[an increasing trend of about 0.21 years per year]{.claim id="c023"}. In the Algarve the series
[shows no clear trend]{.claim id="c024"}.

```{ojs}
ler_data = FileAttachment("q01_life_expectancy_regions.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
smallMultiples(Plotly, ler_data, {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, yTitle: "Life expectancy at birth (years)", lang, alt: "One panel per NUTS II region with life expectancy at birth by three-year period: all rise, the autonomous regions start lower and rise faster, the Algarve fluctuates."})
```

*Chart: life expectancy at birth by NUTS II region (former nomenclature), three-year periods, INE.*

## Question 2 — Healthy life years

Healthy life years (years without activity limitation reported in the EU-SILC survey)
grew in Portugal from [53.9 years at birth in 2004]{.claim id="c025"} to
[64.8 years in 2024]{.claim id="c026"}. In the EU they went from [62.9]{.claim id="c027"} to
[65.2 years]{.claim id="c028"} over the same period. The gap to the EU shrank from
[9.0 years in 2004]{.claim id="c029"} to [0.4 years in 2024]{.claim id="c030"}.

The Portuguese series is, however, very irregular. The trend test
[finds no clear trend (estimated slope of about 0.12 years per year, not significant after correction)]{.claim id="c036"}.
After a high plateau, with [63.6 years in 2012]{.claim id="c251"}, the series falls to
[56.9 years in 2014]{.claim id="c252"}. [The same step repeats in all of Portugal's healthy life years indicators; it has no plausible event and a survey artefact cannot be ruled out, although no source confirms it]{.claim id="c226"}.

[At age 65, healthy life years went from 4.4 in 2004]{.claim id="c031"} to
[9.8 in 2024]{.claim id="c032"}, [with an increasing trend]{.claim id="c037"}, already close to the
European average ([10.3 years in 2024]{.claim id="c033"}). The weight of healthy years in total life
expectancy rose from [68.7% in 2004]{.claim id="c034"} to [78.6% in 2024]{.claim id="c035"}.

Although they live longer, women do not live more years without limitations. In the latest year, the
estimate was [63.9 healthy life years for women in 2024]{.claim id="c038"} and
[65.8 years for men]{.claim id="c039"}, which means that women spend more years with
limitations.

```{ojs}
hly_data = FileAttachment("q02_healthy_life_years.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof hly_ind = Inputs.select(new Map([["Healthy life years at birth", "healthy_life_years|hlth_hle=HLY_Y0"], ["Healthy life years at age 65", "healthy_life_years|hlth_hle=HLY_Y65"], ["Share of life expectancy at birth (%)", "healthy_life_years|hlth_hle=HLY_LE_Y0_PC"], ["Share of life expectancy at age 65 (%)", "healthy_life_years|hlth_hle=HLY_LE_Y65_PC"]]), {label: "Indicator"})
```

```{ojs}
viewof hly_sex = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Total", "T"], ["Women", "F"], ["Men", "M"]]), {value: "T", label: "Sex"})
```

```{ojs}
year_table(hly_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === hly_ind && d.sex === hly_sex), "region", region_labels)
```

*Table: healthy life years (in years) or their share of life expectancy (in %), by year, Portugal and EU, for the chosen indicator and sex (Eurostat).*

## Question 3 — Causes of death

Eurostat's age-standardised rates allow Portugal to be compared with the EU. Mortality
from diseases of the circulatory system fell from [321.67 per hundred thousand in 2011]{.claim id="c040"}
to [220.81 in 2023]{.claim id="c041"}, with
[a decreasing trend of about 7.2 deaths per hundred thousand per year]{.claim id="c055"}. It stayed
well below the European average ([312.95 in 2023]{.claim id="c042"}).

For malignant tumours, the rate went from [246.73 in 2011]{.claim id="c043"} to
[218.22 in 2023]{.claim id="c044"}, with
[a decreasing trend of about 1.4 deaths per hundred thousand per year]{.claim id="c056"}, below the EU
([233.13]{.claim id="c045"}). Almost all of this decline is concentrated in a recent step: the rate
went from [240.46 in 2020]{.claim id="c267"} to [226.14 in 2021]{.claim id="c268"} and stayed
at the new level ([219.51 in 2022]{.claim id="c273"}). The step was left without an associated event (see
Trend changes and events). Diabetes almost halved its rate, from
[44.60 in 2011]{.claim id="c048"} to [23.71 in 2023]{.claim id="c049"}, ending practically at the
European level ([23.53]{.claim id="c050"}).

Respiratory diseases are the main exception: [95.48 per hundred thousand in Portugal]{.claim id="c046"}
against [75.18 in the EU in 2023]{.claim id="c047"}. External causes (accidents, falls, suicide,
among others) [show no clear trend]{.claim id="c057"} and stood at
[45.24 per hundred thousand]{.claim id="c051"}, against [49.40 in the EU]{.claim id="c052"}. Considering all
causes, Portugal recorded [885.63 deaths per hundred thousand in 2023]{.claim id="c053"}, below the EU
([963.42]{.claim id="c054"}).

```{ojs}
cpe_data = FileAttachment("q03_causes_pt_eu.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof cpe_cause = Inputs.select(new Map([["All causes", "all_causes"], ["Circulatory system", "circulatory"], ["Malignant tumours", "cancer_C00_C97"], ["Respiratory system", "respiratory"], ["Diabetes", "diabetes"], ["External causes", "external_causes"]]), {label: "Cause"})
```

```{ojs}
viewof cpe_sex = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Total", "T"], ["Women", "F"], ["Men", "M"]]), {value: "T", label: "Sex"})
```

```{ojs}
year_table(cpe_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === cpe_cause && d.sex === cpe_sex), "region", region_labels)
```

*Table: age-standardised mortality rate, in deaths per hundred thousand inhabitants, by year, Portugal and EU, for the chosen cause and sex (Eurostat).*

### Regional differences

INE data under the new regional nomenclature use a different standard population from Eurostat's,
so the levels are not comparable with those in the previous chart. In this series, Portugal had
[863.9 deaths per hundred thousand in 2024 (all causes)]{.claim id="c060"}. The Autonomous Region of the Azores
stands out with [1161.9]{.claim id="c058"}, followed by [Alentejo with 1011.6]{.claim id="c063"}. Greater
Lisbon had the lowest rate ([820.3]{.claim id="c059"}). For diseases of the circulatory system, the
Azores ([266.9 per hundred thousand]{.claim id="c061"}) almost doubled the Norte
([154.9]{.claim id="c062"}). These are standardised rates, comparable between regions, but in regions with
smaller populations they fluctuate more from year to year. They show where mortality is higher, not why.

```{ojs}
creg_data = FileAttachment("q03_causes_regions.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof creg_cause = Inputs.select(new Map([["Circulatory system", "circulatory"], ["Malignant tumours", "cancer_C00_C97"], ["Respiratory system", "respiratory"], ["Diabetes", "diabetes"], ["External causes", "external_causes"], ["All causes", "all_causes"]]), {label: "Cause"})
```

```{ojs}
heatmap(Plotly, dedupe(creg_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === creg_cause && d.sex === "T"), (d) => d.region + d.date), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, lang, alt: "Heatmap of the standardised rate for the chosen cause by NUTS II region and year: regions with higher rates appear at the top, in darker shades."})
```

*Chart: standardised mortality by cause, NUTS II region and year (Eurostat; the Centro region changes code in the most recent year).*

```{ojs}
c24_data = FileAttachment("q03_causes_regions_2024.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof c24_cause = Inputs.select(new Map([["All causes of death", "Todas as causas de morte"], ["Diseases of the circulatory system", "Doenças do aparelho circulatório"], ["Malignant tumours", "Tumores malignos"], ["Diseases of the respiratory system", "Doenças do aparelho respiratório"], ["Diabetes mellitus", "Diabetes mellitus"], ["External causes of death", "Causas de morte externas"]]), {label: "Cause"})
```

```{ojs}
ranking(Plotly, dedupe(c24_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === c24_cause && d.sex === "HM"), (d) => d.region), {xTitle: "Deaths per 100,000 inhabitants (standardised rate, INE)", highlight: "Portugal", lang, alt: "Regions ranked by the standardised rate for the chosen cause in the most recent year, with Portugal highlighted; the Azores and Alentejo are at the top for every cause."})
```

*Chart: standardised mortality by cause and region, new NUTS nomenclature (INE).*

### Premature mortality

The premature mortality rate (between ages thirty and seventy, from cardiovascular diseases,
cancer, diabetes and chronic respiratory diseases) fell from [357.5 per hundred thousand in 2002]{.claim id="c064"} to
[267.9 in 2024]{.claim id="c065"}, with
[a decreasing trend of about 2.0 per hundred thousand per year]{.claim id="c067"}. In men
([370.8 in 2024]{.claim id="c068"}) it is more than double that in women
([173.3]{.claim id="c069"}). The lowest value in the series was recorded in
[2020, with 258.5]{.claim id="c066"}, an isolated value: the rate was [288.5 in 2019]{.claim id="c263"}
and returned to [277.4 in 2021]{.claim id="c264"}.

[The age-standardised mortality rate before age 75, from all causes, was 320.0 per hundred thousand in 2019]{.claim id="c070"}; it rose to [338.9 in 2021]{.claim id="c071"} and fell again to
[302.8 in 2024]{.claim id="c072"}. This is one of the few indirect signs of the impact of the
pandemic available in these data, and it runs opposite to premature mortality from
chronic diseases, which does not include COVID-19.

```{ojs}
pm_data = FileAttachment("q03_premature_mortality.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof pm_ind = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Premature (ages 30-70)", "premature_mortality_rate_30_70"], ["Before age 75 (standardised)", "standardised_mortality_rate_under75"]]), {value: "premature_mortality_rate_30_70", label: "Indicator"})
```

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, pm_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === pm_ind), {groupBy: "sex", labels: sex_labels, yTitle: "Deaths per 100,000 inhabitants", events: linked_events, lang, alt: "Lines of premature mortality by sex since 2002: a decline with a step in 2004 and an isolated minimum in 2020; in men the level is more than double that of women."})
```

*Chart: premature mortality and standardised mortality before age seventy-five, Portugal (INE).*

## Question 4 — Avoidable mortality and infant mortality

Treatable mortality (deaths that timely and effective health care could prevent) fell from
[94.78 per hundred thousand in 2011]{.claim id="c073"} to [74.24 in 2023]{.claim id="c074"}, with
[a decreasing trend of about 1.8 per hundred thousand per year]{.claim id="c080"}, and is below the EU
average ([86.81]{.claim id="c075"}).

Preventable mortality (deaths avoidable through prevention and public health) went from
[149.25 in 2011]{.claim id="c076"} to [125.94 in 2023]{.claim id="c077"}, but the test
[finds no clear trend]{.claim id="c081"}: there was a peak in
[2021, with 155.89]{.claim id="c079"}. The European average is higher ([150.85 in 2023]{.claim id="c078"}).
The loaded data cover only Portugal and the EU aggregate, which does not allow Portugal to be ranked among
the Member States.

```{ojs}
av_data = FileAttachment("q04_avoidable_mortality.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof av_ind = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Treatable", "treatable"], ["Preventable", "preventable"]]), {value: "treatable", label: "Type"})
```

```{ojs}
viewof av_sex = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Total", "T"], ["Women", "F"], ["Men", "M"]]), {value: "T", label: "Sex"})
```

```{ojs}
smallMultiples(Plotly, av_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === av_ind && d.sex === av_sex), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, cols: 2, yTitle: "Deaths per 100,000 inhabitants", lang, alt: "Two panels with the same axis, Portugal and the EU since 2011, showing treatable or preventable mortality: Portugal below the EU for both types; preventable has a peak in 2021."})
```

*Chart: avoidable mortality (preventable and treatable), one panel for Portugal and one for the EU, with the same vertical axis (Eurostat).*

Infant mortality is one of the biggest transformations in the series: from
[77.5 deaths per thousand live births in 1960]{.claim id="c082"} to [3.0 in 2024]{.claim id="c083"}, with
[a decreasing trend]{.claim id="c088"}. The minimum was [2.4 in 2020]{.claim id="c085"}, and the most
recent value is below the EU average ([3.5 in 2024]{.claim id="c084"}). Neonatal mortality followed the same
path, from [27.9 in 1960]{.claim id="c086"} to [1.8 in 2024]{.claim id="c087"}.

With annual numbers this small, INE publishes a five-year rate for the regions. In the most recent
five-year period, Portugal recorded [2.7 deaths per thousand live births (five years ending in 2025)]{.claim id="c089"}.
The [Centro had 2.1]{.claim id="c090"} and the [Alentejo 2.9]{.claim id="c091"}. In regions with few
births, such as the autonomous regions, a few deaths are enough to move the rate.

```{ojs}
inf_data = FileAttachment("q04_infant_mortality.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof inf_ind = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Infant", "infant"], ["Neonatal", "neonatal"], ["Perinatal", "perinatal"]]), {value: "infant", label: "Indicator"})
```

```{ojs}
timeSeries(Plotly, inf_data.filter((d) => d.indicator === inf_ind), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, yTitle: "Deaths per 1,000 live births", events: linked_events, lang, alt: "Lines of infant, neonatal or perinatal mortality since 1960: a very steep fall in Portugal, which drops below the EU average."})
```

*Chart: infant, neonatal and perinatal mortality, Portugal and EU (Eurostat; the EU only has the infant rate).*

```{ojs}
infr_data = FileAttachment("q04_infant_mortality_regions.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
heatmap(Plotly, dedupe(infr_data, (d) => d.region + d.date), {groupBy: "region", labels: region_labels, lang, alt: "Heatmap of the five-year infant mortality rate by region and last year of the window: the Península de Setúbal and the Azores in darker shades, the Centro and the Norte lighter."})
```

*Chart: five-year infant mortality rate by region and window (INE; the date is the last year of the window).*

## Question 5 — Excess mortality during the pandemic

This question was not answered. Both planned Eurostat sources failed the access test.
Weekly mortality by region [timed out in the test without returning a result]{.claim id="c092"},
and monthly excess mortality [returned a server error]{.claim id="c093"}. By a decision
recorded in the study, the analysis went ahead without this component and
[weekly excess mortality is declared as not covered]{.claim id="c094"}. The only indirect
signs in these data are the drop in life expectancy at the start of the pandemic and the
temporary rise in mortality before age seventy-five (Question 1 and Question 3).

## Question 6 — Morbidity and self-rated health

The share of people aged sixteen or over who report a chronic disease or long-standing health problem
rose from [32.1% in 2004]{.claim id="c095"} to [44.1% in 2025]{.claim id="c096"},
[an increasing trend of about 0.7 percentage points per year]{.claim id="c097"}. A good part of
this rise is concentrated in a short ramp: from [34.7% in 2011]{.claim id="c240"} to
[42.7% in 2015]{.claim id="c241"}, passing through [39.7% in 2013]{.claim id="c269"} and
[40.3% in 2014]{.claim id="c270"}. [The corrected detector confirms a real step, dated 2013, in the middle of the ramp, and repeated in all groups]{.claim id="c276"};
there is no isolated jump in the following year. Among
people aged sixty-five or over the pattern repeats, from [66.7% in 2011]{.claim id="c244"}
to [72.5% in 2015]{.claim id="c245"}. [This ramp coincided with the adjustment programme, but an effect of the survey method cannot be ruled out]{.claim id="c215"}
(see Trend changes and events). After that
there is no jump: [41.5% in 2018]{.claim id="c242"} and [41.2% in 2019]{.claim id="c243"}. By region, the
highest values are in [Madeira (47.5% in 2025)]{.claim id="c098"} and in the
[Centro (46.8%)]{.claim id="c099"}, and the lowest in the [Algarve (38.5%)]{.claim id="c100"}.

At the same time, self-rated health improved. According to INE, the share who consider their health
bad or very bad fell from [21.1% in 2004]{.claim id="c101"} to [12.1% in 2025]{.claim id="c102"}
([decreasing trend]{.claim id="c107"}), and the share who consider it good or very good rose from
[45.4%]{.claim id="c103"} to [52.7%]{.claim id="c104"}. The latter fell from
[49.7% in 2011]{.claim id="c246"} to [46.0% in 2014]{.claim id="c247"} and then recovered
gradually, to [49.3% in 2018]{.claim id="c248"} and [50.1% in 2019]{.claim id="c249"}, with no step in those
two years. The improvement is greater among older people: the share with bad or very bad health
[among people aged 65 or over went from 55.2% in 2004]{.claim id="c105"}
to [28.1% in 2025]{.claim id="c106"}.

More declared chronic disease and better self-rating can coexist, for example with more
diagnoses and better-controlled diseases, but these data do not allow the explanations to be told apart.

In the European comparison (EU-SILC), Portugal still lags behind. In the latest year,
[52.6% of Portuguese people rated their health as good or very good in 2025]{.claim id="c108"}, against
[67.9% in the EU]{.claim id="c109"}, and [12.2% as bad or very bad]{.claim id="c110"}, against
[8.8% in the EU]{.claim id="c111"}. In Portugal the latter share was [20.3% in 2010]{.claim id="c112"}
and fell to [18.0% in 2011]{.claim id="c250"}, in a step that held. Later there is no
jump: [15.5% in 2018]{.claim id="c271"} and [15.2% in 2019]{.claim id="c272"}. Overall, the series has a
[decreasing trend of about 0.5 percentage points per year]{.claim id="c113"}.

```{ojs}
chr_data = FileAttachment("q06_chronic_condition.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof chr_age = Inputs.radio(new Map([["16+", "16+"], ["16 - 64 years", "16 - 64 anos"], ["65 and over", "65 e mais anos"]]), {value: "16+", label: "Age"})
```

```{ojs}
smallMultiples(Plotly, chr_data.filter((d) => d.age === chr_age), {groupBy: "sex", labels: sex_labels, yTitle: "% of the population", lang, alt: "One panel per sex, with the same axis, showing the share with a chronic disease since 2004: a rise concentrated between 2011 and 2015 and stability afterwards; women above men."})
```

*Chart: population with a chronic disease or long-standing health problem, one panel per sex, for the chosen age (INE).*

```{ojs}
chrr_data = FileAttachment("q06_chronic_condition_regions.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
viewof chrr_year = Inputs.radio(new Map([["2025", "2025-01-01"], ["2024", "2024-01-01"]]), {value: "2025-01-01", label: "Year"})
```

## Question 7 — Risk factors

The risk factor data come from the National Health Survey. Tobacco and body mass index
exist only for the most recent wave, and alcohol has three waves. The loaded data contain no
comparison with the EU or information on physical activity.

[In 2025, 12.7% of the population aged fifteen or over smoked daily]{.claim id="c114"}. Among
men the share was [17.3%]{.claim id="c115"} and among women [8.4%]{.claim id="c116"}. The
[Algarve (18.2%)]{.claim id="c117"} and the [Azores (18.1%)]{.claim id="c118"} had the highest
shares, and the [Centro (10.5%)]{.claim id="c119"} the lowest. About
[61.9% of the population had never smoked]{.claim id="c120"}.

Obesity affected [17.4% of adults in 2025]{.claim id="c121"}.

Among those who drank alcohol in the previous twelve months, the share who had at least one occasion of
six or more drinks rose from [33.2% in 2014]{.claim id="c122"} to [42.8% in 2019]{.claim id="c123"}
and stood at [42.5% in 2025]{.claim id="c124"}. Among young people [aged 15 to 24 it went from 45.7% in 2014]{.claim id="c125"}
to [66.2% in 2025]{.claim id="c126"}. With only three waves no trend test is done, and the
survey waves do not use exactly the same method.

## Question 8 — Mental health

The longest comparable series is that of suicide. The rate was
[11.6 per hundred thousand inhabitants in 2002]{.claim id="c127"}, reached [11.7 in 2014]{.claim id="c128"} and
stood at [9.0 in 2024]{.claim id="c129"}; the test [finds no clear trend]{.claim id="c130"}.
In men the rate is more than three times that of women ([15.5]{.claim id="c131"} against
[4.4 in 2022]{.claim id="c132"}). Among people aged seventy-five or over, the rate fell from
[33.5 in 2002]{.claim id="c133"} to [20.0 in 2024]{.claim id="c134"}. The national series joins two
INE tables (old nomenclature up to one year, new afterwards), and the join may affect
comparability. There is a level break at the start of the series, without an associated event (see Trend
changes and events).

For depressive symptoms, the share of people with no symptoms fell from
[88.7% in 2014]{.claim id="c135"} to [83.5% in 2025]{.claim id="c136"}, and the share with
severe symptoms went from [3.7%]{.claim id="c137"} to [4.3%]{.claim id="c138"}. With three waves and different
survey methods, this is an indication and not a demonstrated trend. Antidepressant consumption and the
mental health modules of the European survey were not part of the loaded data.

## Question 9 — Unmet care needs

Unmet needs due to cost, distance or waiting list are considered here. For
medical care, the share in Portugal went from [1.1% in 2008]{.claim id="c139"} to
[3.3% in 2012]{.claim id="c140"}, in the crisis years, and stood at [2.5% in 2025]{.claim id="c141"},
close to the European average ([2.4%]{.claim id="c142"}). Over the full series
[there is no clear trend]{.claim id="c154"}.

For dental care, the problem is bigger: [7.3% in 2008]{.claim id="c143"}, a peak of
[14.6% in 2015]{.claim id="c144"} and [7.9% in 2025]{.claim id="c145"}, against
[3.3% in the EU]{.claim id="c146"}. Here too [there is no clear trend over the full series]{.claim id="c155"}.
The gap to the EU widened abruptly: Portugal went from [9.1% in 2011]{.claim id="c253"}
to [13.8% in 2012]{.claim id="c254"}, and the difference from the European average from
[3.8 percentage points]{.claim id="c255"} to [8.4]{.claim id="c256"}. [That jump coincided with the adjustment programme]{.claim id="c219"}
and [also coincided with the revision of user charges]{.claim id="c220"}; no source establishes
the relationship (see Trend changes and events).

Inequality by income is very marked. In the lowest income quintile, unmet dental
needs reached [27.6% in 2015]{.claim id="c147"} and stood at
[16.9% in 2025]{.claim id="c148"}, against [1.6% in the highest quintile]{.claim id="c149"}. For medical
care, they were [4.2% in the lowest quintile]{.claim id="c150"} and [1.0% in the highest in 2025]{.claim id="c151"}.
Among those below the at-risk-of-poverty threshold the total share was
[7.5%]{.claim id="c152"}, against [3.3% above the threshold]{.claim id="c153"}.

## Question 10 — Health system expenditure and resources

Current health expenditure rose from [8.62% of GDP in 2000]{.claim id="c156"} to a peak of
[11.22% in 2021]{.claim id="c157"} and stood at [10.20% in 2024]{.claim id="c158"}, at the EU level
([10.16%]{.claim id="c159"}). The jump to the peak began with the pandemic: from
[9.61% in 2019]{.claim id="c261"} to [10.64% in 2020]{.claim id="c262"}. A percentage of GDP
also depends on the denominator, which is not part of the loaded data, so this jump should not be
read only as more spending. Per inhabitant, in purchasing power standards, Portugal spent
[3247.42 in 2024]{.claim id="c160"}, against [4074.88 in the EU]{.claim id="c161"}.

The financing structure sets Portugal apart. Households' out-of-pocket payments accounted for
[28.67% of current expenditure in 2024]{.claim id="c162"}, almost double the EU
([15.06%]{.claim id="c163"}), and their weight has an [increasing trend of about 0.23 percentage points per year]{.claim id="c166"}.
The series has a step from [26.70% in 2011]{.claim id="c257"} to [29.66% in 2012]{.claim id="c258"},
and a one-off fall from [30.20% in 2019]{.claim id="c259"} to [27.61% in 2020]{.claim id="c260"}.
Public and compulsory financing covered [61.88%]{.claim id="c164"}, against
[80.33% in the EU]{.claim id="c165"}.

The number of physicians licensed to practise went from
[75.65 per hundred thousand inhabitants in 1960]{.claim id="c167"} to [591.35 in 2024]{.claim id="c168"}. This
concept includes physicians who do not practise and overstates active physicians. Practising nurses
went from [422.29 in 2004]{.claim id="c169"} to [767.54 in 2024]{.claim id="c170"}. The
growth of nurses slowed, and [this change of pace coincided with the start of the adjustment programme]{.claim id="c225"}: it went from
[about 25 per hundred thousand between 2009 and 2010]{.claim id="c274"} to
[about 10 between 2011 and 2012]{.claim id="c275"}. The physicians series accelerates at the end of the first
decade of the century, without an associated event (see Trend changes and events).

Hospital beds fell from [395.92 per hundred thousand in 1985]{.claim id="c171"} to
[330.98 in 2024]{.claim id="c172"}, well below the European average ([507.35]{.claim id="c173"}).
Differences between regions are large. In the latest year available, the Norte had
[561.01 physicians per hundred thousand]{.claim id="c174"} and the Alentejo [322.33]{.claim id="c175"}; Madeira had
[793.69 beds per hundred thousand]{.claim id="c176"} and the Alentejo [213.18]{.claim id="c177"}. Beds
are counted where the hospitals are, not where the patients who use them live.

## Trend changes and events

[An earlier version of this study was withdrawn because the break detector had an error; the breaks and the links to events were redone with the corrected detector]{.claim id="c211"}.
The detector looks for level steps (regression with trend and step, with an F test), slope changes
(on annual differences) and isolated peaks. It found
[29 candidate breaks: 10 coincided with verified events, in 12 links all of grade C, and 19 were left without an event]{.claim id="c210"}.
For each break, a dated event with a confirmed primary source was sought within a plausible
window. No source consulted establishes that any of these events caused a change in the
series, so the text speaks only of temporal coincidence.

### Events considered

- [The Memorandum of Understanding with the European Commission, the ECB and the IMF was signed in May 2011, included measures to contain health spending, and the programme ended in May 2014]{.claim id="c179"}.
- [Decree-Law No. 113/2011, of 29 November, regulated access to NHS services, including user charges and special regimes]{.claim id="c212"}.
- [The World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 March 2020]{.claim id="c180"}.
- [Law No. 37/2007, of 14 August, set out tobacco prevention rules, including the ban on smoking in enclosed public spaces]{.claim id="c213"}.

### Links found (all grade C)

**Adjustment programme and user charges.**

- [The ramp in declared chronic disease, dated 2013, coincided with the adjustment programme; no source establishes a relationship and a survey method artefact cannot be ruled out]{.claim id="c215"}.
- [The same 2013 step in chronic disease among people aged 65 or over coincided with the adjustment programme; a survey method artefact cannot be ruled out]{.claim id="c216"}.
- [The fall in self-reported good or very good health, dated 2013, coincided with the adjustment programme; no causal source and a survey method artefact not ruled out]{.claim id="c217"}.
- [The 2011 break in self-reported bad health in EU-SILC coincided with the start of the adjustment programme; no causal source and a survey method artefact not ruled out]{.claim id="c218"}.
- [The 2012 widening of the gap to the EU in unmet dental needs coincided with the adjustment programme; no source establishes the relationship]{.claim id="c219"}.
- [The same 2012 widening coincided with the revision of user charges; the decree regulates access to the NHS, but describes no mechanism or effect on unmet dental needs]{.claim id="c220"}.
- [The 2012 increase in the weight of out-of-pocket payments in current expenditure coincided with the adjustment programme; no source establishes the relationship]{.claim id="c222"}.
- [The same 2012 increase in out-of-pocket payments coincided with the revision of user charges; the source describes no mechanism or effect]{.claim id="c223"}.
- [The 2011 slope change in practising nurses coincided with the start of the adjustment programme; no source consulted establishes a relationship]{.claim id="c225"}.

**COVID-19 pandemic.**

- [The isolated 2020 minimum in premature mortality from chronic diseases coincided with the first year of the pandemic; the direction of the change (a fall) is unexpected and no source establishes the relationship]{.claim id="c214"}.
- [The 2020 step in health expenditure as a percentage of GDP coincided with the pandemic; the indicator also depends on GDP, the denominator, and no source consulted quantifies the effect]{.claim id="c221"}.
- [The one-off 2020 fall in the weight of households' out-of-pocket payments coincided with the pandemic; no causal source]{.claim id="c224"}.

### Survey series: what was confirmed

Chronic disease, self-rated health and healthy life years come from surveys, and a step
may reflect a change of method rather than a real change.
[The review requested for the study flagged probable steps in the survey series in 2014 (chronic disease) and in 2018 and 2019 (self-rated health from INE and EU-SILC)]{.claim id="c277"}.
With the corrected detector, it was checked, series by series, whether and in which years these steps exist, instead
of discarding them:

- **Chronic disease (INE).** [The step is confirmed, but dated 2013, in the middle of a ramp between 2011 and 2015; neither chronic disease nor self-rated health from INE and EU-SILC has a jump in 2018 or 2019]{.claim id="c236"}.
  The series rises from [34.7% in 2011]{.claim id="c240"} to [42.7% in 2015]{.claim id="c241"} over
  several years, without an isolated jump in the flagged year ([39.7% in 2013]{.claim id="c269"},
  [40.3% in 2014]{.claim id="c270"}), and is stable afterwards ([41.5% in 2018]{.claim id="c242"}, [41.2% in 2019]{.claim id="c243"}).
- **Good or very good health (INE).** A fall is confirmed, from [49.7% in 2011]{.claim id="c246"}
  to [46.0% in 2014]{.claim id="c247"}, followed by gradual recovery, with no step in
  [2018 (49.3%)]{.claim id="c248"} or in [2019 (50.1%)]{.claim id="c249"}.
- **Bad or very bad health (EU-SILC).** The only step is between [2010 (20.3%)]{.claim id="c112"} and
  [2011 (18.0%)]{.claim id="c250"}; in [2018 (15.5%)]{.claim id="c271"} and
  [2019 (15.2%)]{.claim id="c272"} there is no jump.
- **Healthy life years (EU-SILC).** The mid-decade fall is also confirmed and is dealt with in Breaks without an event.

The confirmed steps do not fall in the years flagged in the review, but this does not prove that they are
real changes in the population's health: the links to the adjustment programme are only temporal, a method
artefact is not ruled out, and no source confirms or excludes it.

### Breaks without an event

These cases are results of the analysis, not failures.

- **Healthy life years.** After [63.6 years in 2012]{.claim id="c251"}, the series falls to
  [56.9 in 2014]{.claim id="c252"}, with the same pattern in all indicators; [no plausible event, and a survey artefact cannot be ruled out]{.claim id="c226"}.
- **Life expectancy and infant mortality in the last century.** [Left without an event were the 1961 peaks in female life expectancy and infant mortality, the 1966 break in women's life expectancy at 65, the 1967 steps in neonatal and perinatal mortality, the 1972 breaks in female life expectancy and infant mortality, and the slope changes of 1984 in infant mortality, 1994 in neonatal and 1997 in perinatal]{.claim id="c227"}.
  [For the 1972 breaks there were candidates, such as the 1971 reform of the health centres, but without a legible and verified primary source]{.claim id="c228"}.
  [The 1965 slope change in EU infant mortality fell outside the scope of national events]{.claim id="c237"}.
- **Premature mortality.** The rate went from [346.1 in 2003]{.claim id="c265"} to
  [322.4 in 2004]{.claim id="c266"}; [it is a fall of unusual size, without a plausible event and with a possible series artefact, not confirmed]{.claim id="c230"}.
- **Malignant tumours.** The standardised rate went from [240.46 in 2020]{.claim id="c267"} to
  [226.14 in 2021]{.claim id="c268"} and stayed at that level in [2022 (219.51)]{.claim id="c273"};
  [the step was left without an associated event]{.claim id="c231"}. A change in cause coding
  or method was not investigated and remains a possible, unconfirmed explanation.
- **Suicide.** [The 2005 level break in the suicide rate was left without a plausible event; the series was spliced and comparability remains to be confirmed]{.claim id="c232"}.
- **Resources.** [The 2001 level drop in hospital beds was left without an event, with a possible change of definition not confirmed]{.claim id="c233"}, and
  [the 2008 slope change in licensed physicians was also left without an event]{.claim id="c234"}.

### Events without a visible effect

- [The 2007 tobacco law does not coincide with any break in the series analysed between 2007 and 2012, and the 2004 break in premature mortality predates the law]{.claim id="c235"}.
  This does not mean the law had no effect: the available series may lack the sensitivity
  to detect it, and there is no annual tobacco consumption series in the loaded data.

## Associations between indicators

Spearman correlations were tested between the annual changes of pairs of national series from
different charts, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple testing. Using annual differences
prevents two series from appearing associated just because both rise over time.
[45 pairs were tested and none remained significant after the correction]{.claim id="c209"}. This
is a result: there are no robust associations between indicators in these data. Even if there were,
they would be associations and not causes, and some could be mechanical, for example between a part and
its total.

## Methodology

- **Data.** All series come from INE and Eurostat tables, downloaded by code and
  normalised to a long format (date, region, sex, age, indicator, value, unit) in
  `data/clean/`. The National Health Survey proportions (tobacco, body mass index,
  alcohol, depressive symptoms) were calculated as the count of the category divided by the total of the
  same table.
- **Trends.** The annual slope is estimated with the Theil-Sen estimator, which is robust to
  extreme values. Significance is tested with Mann-Kendall and corrected for multiple testing. The text only
  says "increasing trend" or "decreasing trend" when the test confirms it; otherwise it says "no clear
  trend".
- **Breaks.** Level steps are detected with a trend-plus-step regression (F test
  and effect size), slope changes with the PELT algorithm on annual differences, and
  isolated peaks with a robust z-score. For each break, a dated event with a primary source
  confirmed by code was sought within a plausible window. The grade of evidence (A, B or C)
  sets the language used; in this study all links are grade C.
- **Comparison with the EU.** The Eurostat aggregate of the twenty-seven Member States is used whenever it exists in the loaded
  data.
- **Regions.** Regional series use the NUTS nomenclature in which the source publishes them. The new
  nomenclature splits the former Lisbon Metropolitan Area and redraws the Centro and Alentejo, so
  the series under the two nomenclatures appear in separate charts and are not compared as if they were
  the same regions. Regional comparisons use rates, never counts.

## Limitations

- **Excess mortality not covered.** By a decision recorded in the study,
  [weekly excess mortality was not covered]{.claim id="c094"}: the weekly mortality source
  [timed out in the test]{.claim id="c092"} and the monthly excess mortality source
  [returned a server error]{.claim id="c093"}. Question 5 remains unanswered.
- **Surveys and method artefacts.** Chronic disease, self-rated health and healthy life years
  depend on surveys. The steps found in these series
  ([see Survey series]{.claim id="c236"}) may reflect changes of method; the links to
  events are only temporal. The National Health Survey indicators have few waves
  (tobacco and body mass index only one), which prevents trend tests and comparison with the EU.
- **Unconfirmed events.** [Three catalogued events were not confirmed by code and are not cited as facts: the creation of the NHS in 1979, the severe 2014/2015 flu season in Europe and the expansion of the oral health programme between 2016 and 2018]{.claim id="c229"}.
  They are left out of the links and of the list of events without effect.
- **National and European sources are not directly comparable.** INE and Eurostat standardised rates
  use different standard populations.
- **Health personnel.** Physicians are counted as "licensed to practise", which overstates
  active physicians.
- **Scope not covered.** No data were loaded on antidepressant consumption, mental
  health modules of the European survey, physical activity, life expectancy by education, or
  Portugal's position among Member States (only the EU aggregate). Socioeconomic
  inequalities were analysed only by income, in unmet needs.
- **Spliced suicide series.** The national series joins two INE tables with different
  regional nomenclatures.
- **Provisional values.** The most recent years of several Eurostat series may be revised.
